bilingual_alignment.assessment: Both versions assert the existence of a transcendental alpha whose partial-quotient sequence is Sturmian, explicitly specifying complexity n+1. The final parenthesis is explanatory motivation and introduces no additional mathematical requirement.

qualification: The claim is sufficiently standard and definite for a faithful mathematical submission under the usual real regular-continued-fraction and one-sided Sturmian-word conventions. No substantive ambiguity requires source deferral. This is a judgment about the meaning of the source only, not about its truth, difficulty, novelty, or solvability.

faithful_conventions_to_state.convention: Alpha is a real number, and transcendental means that it is not a zero of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients. The real domain is the ordinary context of the unqualified partial-quotient terminology here.

Use the regular (simple) continued fraction alpha = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], with a_0 an integer and a_j a positive integer for j >= 1. The word being tested is the infinite fractional-part word a_1 a_2 a_3 ...; its positions may be relabeled starting at zero without changing which entries form the word.

Use one-sided infinite words. For each integer n >= 1, p(n) is the cardinality of the set of contiguous length-n blocks (a_j, ..., a_{j+n-1}) with j >= 1, and the exact requirement is p(n) = n+1 for every n >= 1. Including n = 0 with the unique empty word is an equivalent counting convention.

Letters are partial-quotient values, hence positive integers. A binary alphabet means two distinct such values, not the literal symbols 0 and 1. The source fixes neither their values nor an auxiliary slope, intercept, or particular word.

routine_convention_notes: The source leaves the initial index implicit. Separating the integer part a_0 and explicitly testing the fractional-part word is the standard convention used for this qualification. Any different choice of the tested word must be made explicit; arbitrary prefix insertion or deletion must not be treated as a mere relabeling of indices.

The explicit complexity n+1 selects ordinary factor complexity, not the number of prefixes, a limiting or asymptotic complexity, an eventually valid equality, or a complexity after a noninjective coding.
The terms real and regular are conventional contextual expansions of partial-quotient sequence, not an authorization to replace the claim by a generalized continued-fraction problem.
rules_considered: The source exists in both languages and their mathematical requirements agree.
The rules require a solution report and Lean project to match the conjecture definitions; the explicit conventions above make the intended target reviewable.

The rules require necessary conditions and clear definitions. Standard named definitions plus the stated exact complexity are adequate here; routine equivalent notation alone is not grounds for rejection.
